title: One-Variable Data, Part 3: Traps and the Fast Way

beats.say: In this video, we look at five mistakes students make with one-variable data, and then use Desmos to compute the mean of a frequency table in one line.
Each trap is shown as a wrong line first, then the right line, with the reason it is so tempting.
Trap one. In a frequency table, students average the values column, and ignore how often each value occurs.
Each value must be weighted by its frequency. The total is thirty books over twenty students, so the mean is one point five.
beats.right_why: Weight each value by its frequency

beats.say: Trap two. The median is the middle of the sorted list. A student who takes the middle of the list as it was given gets the wrong value.
Sort first. The list becomes three, five, eight, nine, twelve, and the middle value is eight.
Trap three. When two groups have different sizes, the combined mean is not the midpoint of their means.
Use totals. Twelve times seventy plus eighteen times eighty is twenty-two hundred eighty, divided by thirty, which is seventy-six.
beats.right_why: Add totals, divide by the count

scenes.title: Trap 4: extreme values and the median

beats.say: Trap four. Making the largest value even larger does not change the median of a list with an odd number of values.
beats.wrong: raise the max: the median rises

beats.say: The median stays the same, but the range and the standard deviation both increase, since the data is more spread out.
beats.right: median same; range and SD grow

beats.say: Trap five. The lists forty, forty-five, fifty, fifty-five, sixty, and forty-eight through fifty-two, have the same mean and the same median. Students assume they must have the same spread.
The first list is much more spread out, so its standard deviation is much larger. Mean and median describe the center, and the standard deviation describes the spread.
Desmos does list statistics in one line. For a frequency table, type the values and the frequencies as two lists, then compute the weighted mean.
Our example is the books table. The values are zero to four, and the frequencies are four, seven, five, three, and one.
Open a fresh graph. We will store the values in a list named V, and the frequencies in a list named F.
Type V equals the list of values, zero, one, two, three, four, inside square brackets.
Now type F equals the list of frequencies, four, seven, five, three, one.
Type total of V times F, over total of F. Multiplying two lists multiplies them entry by entry, which weights each value by its frequency.
Desmos reports one point five, which matches our answer by hand. The fast method gave the weighted mean in one line.

Now a practice problem. Six numbers have a mean of fifteen. Five of them are twelve, eighteen, fourteen, sixteen, and ten. What is the sixth number? Pause the video, try it, and then watch the solution.
When a mean is known, think in totals. Six numbers with a mean of fifteen have a total of six times fifteen.
Six times fifteen is ninety. So the six numbers must add up to ninety.
The five known numbers add up to seventy. The missing number is the total, ninety, minus the sum of the known numbers.
Twelve plus eighteen plus fourteen plus sixteen plus ten is seventy, so the known numbers add up to seventy.
Ninety minus seventy is twenty. So the sixth number must be twenty, to make the total ninety.
Check by adding the sixth number. Seventy plus twenty is ninety, and ninety divided by six is fifteen. That is the mean we were given.
To recap. Weight a frequency table by its frequencies, sort before finding the median, and combine groups with totals.
Extreme values move the mean and the spread, but not the median. Mean and median describe the center, not the spread.
Use Desmos for lists and weighted means. In the next topic, we study two-variable data.
